t: 19.11 A 13GHz Charge-Pump PLL Achieving 15.8fsrms Integrated Jitter and -98.5dBc Reference Spur
pb: Modern RF-sampling communication systems (wideband data converters, complex modulation) impose stringent phase-locked loop (PLL) requirements: ultra-low jitter and near-zero reference spurs. Sub-sampling PLLs achieve superior low-frequency phase noise but suffer large reference spurs from BFSK effects. Sampling PLLs avoid periodic VCO modulation but are limited by available loop gain (K_stope). Charge-pump PLLs dominate industry but their in-band phase noise, set by charge-pump characteristics, makes ultra-low jitter challenging.
me: A dual-path charge-pump PLL architecture integrating: (1) Resistive-discharge time-amplifying phase-frequency detector (RD-TAPFD) improving charge-pump linearity, (2) Series-resonance VCO (SR-VCO) with over-voltage protection suppressing phase noise, (3) Sampling-based filter achieving sharp low-pass response without large capacitors. The dual-path design balances in-band phase noise suppression via increased phase-detector gain while maintaining robust lock acquisition.
nv: Dual-path charge-pump PLL with resistive-discharge TAPFD and series-resonance VCO achieving record 15.8fs integrated jitter and -98.5dBc reference spur at 13GHz.

mx.other: Integrated jitter: 15.8fsrms, Reference spur: -98.5dBc, Center freq: 13GHz

th: Dual-path charge-pump PLL with ultra-low jitter and spur suppression

t: 36.5 A Low-Latency 200Gb/s PAM-4 Heterogeneous Transceiver in 0.13µm SiGe BiCMOS and 28nm CMOS for Retimed Pluggable Optics
pb: AI infrastructure demands 200G/lane serial links for data-center interconnects, but linear-drive pluggable optics (LPO) face severe challenges at 200G: very-short-reach (VSR) channel insertion loss increases by 14dB at 2x data rate (to -14dB overall), and retimed LPO solutions (with DSP) introduce unacceptable latency (incompatible with low-latency AI inference requirements). Traditional 200G retimed schemes mitigate 30dB insertion loss via DSP compensation, but this adds significant pipeline delay.
me: A heterogeneous transceiver architecture combining SiGe BiCMOS analog front-end (0.13µm) and 28nm CMOS digital logic. The key innovation is a non-ADC-based receiver eliminating the DSP delay bottleneck. Analog equalization on the SiGe side handles severe VSR channel insertion loss without requiring DSP; 28nm CMOS integrates clock/data recovery and link-layer functions. This heterogeneous approach achieves comparable energy efficiency to retimed solutions while maintaining near-zero additional latency.
nv: Heterogeneous 0.13µm SiGe + 28nm CMOS transceiver achieving 200G/lane transmission with non-ADC receiver architecture, eliminating DSP latency penalty for AI-centric low-latency interconnects.

mx.speedup: 200Gb/s, low-latency (non-ADC)
mx.other: SiGe 0.13µm + CMOS 28nm heterogeneous integration

th: Low-latency 200Gb/s heterogeneous transceiver for AI data-center links

t: A 56-to-64GHz Linear Power Amplifier with 30.2dBm Psat and 23.5% PAEpeak Using Scalable Matched-Zone-Expanding Radial Power Combining with EM-Loss Reduction in 40nm Bulk CMOS
pb: High mm-wave frequencies (V-band, 56–64GHz) for 5G NR FR2-2 and SATCOM require high-power, high-efficiency power amplifiers in voltage-limited silicon processes. Traditional voltage-mode and current-mode power combining face impedance mismatches as combining scales (Zopt changes with combining ratio), limiting PA core selection. Passive combiner losses increase significantly with scale due to routing parasitics, and transistor efficiency degrades at high mm-wave due to parasitic capacitance and fT/fmax limitations.
me: A 56–64GHz linear PA with scalable matched-zone-expanding radial power combiner. Key techniques: (1) Radial combining geometry reducing layout parasitics and combiner loss compared to linear topologies, (2) Matched-zone expansion maintaining constant impedance transformation ratio across combining stages, enabling flexible PA core selection regardless of combining scale, (3) EM-loss reduction via optimized routing and parasitic minimization, (4) Segmented PA cores and efficient waveform shaping for 23.5% PAE.
nv: Scalable matched-zone-expanding radial power combiner with EM-loss reduction enabling high-efficiency, high-power mm-wave PA at V-band frequencies without impedance mismatch degradation.

mx.speedup: 30.2dBm Psat
mx.other: Frequency range: 56–64GHz, V-band

t: 5.7 A 4.7GHz, 27.7dBm Pout, 37.8% PAE, 5.8° AM-PM Distortion Polar SCPA Using In-Cell Fast Slope-to-Phase Self-Calibration and Asymmetrical 4-to-1 Differential Power-Combining Transformer
pb: Digital power amplifiers (DPAs) for sub-6G and WiFi applications require high output power, high efficiency, and low linearity distortion to support complex modulation (high-order QAM). Conventional DPAs need additional digital pre-distortion (DPD) modules increasing area and power consumption. Voltage-mode switched-capacitor power amplifiers (SCPAs) improve linearity but suffer AM-PM (amplitude-to-phase) distortion at high frequencies due to transistor switching delays affecting waveform shape and phase response.
me: A polar switched-capacitor power amplifier (SCPA) with in-cell fast slope-to-phase self-calibration. Key techniques: (1) Edge detectors in each unit cell detect rising/falling edge delays in switching waveforms, (2) Slope-to-phase tuner adjusts edges in real-time to compensate for phase distortion, (3) Asymmetrical 4-to-1 differential power-combining transformer balancing impedance and efficiency, (4) Fast calibration loop (low loop delay) enabling sub-modulation-period response for wideband signal support.
nv: In-cell fast slope-to-phase self-calibration enabling AM-PM linearity improvement in high-frequency SCPA without external DPD, supporting complex modulation directly.

mx.speedup: 27.7dBm output power
mx.other: Frequency: 4.7GHz, eliminates external DPD

th: Self-calibrating switched-capacitor power amplifier for high-linearity wireless TX

t: A 64Gb/s/wire 10.5Tb/s/mm/Layer Single-Ended Simultaneous Bi-Directional Transceiver with Echo and Crosstalk Cancellation for a Die-to-Die Interface in 28nm CMOS
pb: Die-to-die (chiplet) interfaces demand ultra-high edge density and low BER; simultaneous bi-directional (SBD) signaling doubles data rate but introduces echo (near-end reflection) and crosstalk (NEXT/FEXT). Existing echo-cancellation circuits are power-hungry; removing ground shielding for density gains increases crosstalk vulnerability.
me: Single-ended SBD transceiver with integrated analog echo cancellation (EC), near-end crosstalk (NEXT), and far-end crosstalk (FEXT) cancellation. Shield-less channel design (ground shielding removed). Three-layer cancellation approach: EC suppresses echo from local transmitter; NEXT/FEXT cancellation handles coupling from aggressor wires on same die.
nv: Combined echo + NEXT + FEXT cancellation in single transceiver for shield-less SBD die-to-die signaling.
th: High-density shield-less die-to-die transceiver with multi-source cancellation

t: A 1.11pJ/b 224Gb/s XSR Receiver with Slice-Based CTLE and PI-Based Clock Generator in 12nm CMOS
pb: Extra-short reach (XSR) 224Gb/s receivers at 112Gb/s-equivalent require both CTLE bandwidth doubling and 8x sampling frequency increase while maintaining strict power and area constraints.
me: Extra-short reach receiver using slice-based continuous-time linear equalizer (CTLE) and phase-interpolator (PI)-based eight-phase clock generator, enabling efficient bandwidth scaling in 12nm CMOS. Slicing CTLE distributes filtering across multiple stages.
nv: Slice-based CTLE architecture enabling efficient bandwidth scaling to 224Gb/s while maintaining power efficiency (1.11pJ/bit).
th: 224Gb/s extra-short reach receiver with slice-based equalization

t: 36.6 A 112Gb/s 0.61pJ/b PAM-4 Linear TIA Supporting Extended PD-TIA Reach in 28nm CMOS
pb: Co-packaged optical receivers require extended photodiode-to-TIA reach (0.2 inch vs. 0.03 inch in prior work) for thermal, mechanical, and field-replacement flexibility, but long interconnects introduce signal reflection, in-band amplitude un-flatness, and bandwidth degradation.
me: A 4×112Gb/s PAM-4 linear TIA employs active-input-termination (AIT-TIA) to suppress reflection and signal-interpolation-based single-ended-to-differential converter (S2D) for enhanced bandwidth. These techniques extend achievable PD-TIA reach to 0.2 inch with 0.61pJ/b energy efficiency in 28nm CMOS.
nv: Active-input-termination TIA with signal-interpolation S2D converter enabling 0.2-inch PD-TIA reach while maintaining low power efficiency (0.61pJ/b).

mx.other: 112Gb/s data rate, 0.2-inch PD-TIA reach

th: Extended-reach TIA via active input termination

t: LEGOSim: A Unified Parallel Simulation Framework for Multi-chiplet Heterogeneous Integration
pb: Simulating heterogeneous multi-chiplet systems (e.g., CPU+GPU+CIM chiplets integrated on an interposer) is not supported by existing simulators (gem5, GPGPU-Sim) because they lack modular composition of heterogeneous chiplet models and suffer from prohibitive synchronization overhead in parallel simulation—per-cycle global synchronization can waste up to 99.9% of simulation time on barrier overhead.
me: LEGOSim wraps individual chiplet simulators (open-source or proprietary) as parallel OS processes called 'simlets', each advancing independently using a PDES (parallel discrete event simulation) approach. An on-demand synchronization protocol uses adaptive time quanta and non-global fencing: synchronization only occurs when a simlet needs to send or receive a message whose timestamp falls within another simlet's current quantum, avoiding unnecessary global barriers. A Network-on-Interposer (NoI) simulator models inter-chiplet communication (latency, bandwidth, topology) and is integrated as a separate simlet. The framework was validated against SIMBA (multi-chiplet neural network accelerator) and a CiM-based accelerator, achieving average errors of 3.79% and 3.94% respectively.
nv: The on-demand, non-global synchronization protocol with adaptive time quanta that allows heterogeneous chiplet simlets to advance asynchronously and only synchronize when cross-chiplet message delivery actually requires it, reducing synchronization overhead by up to 99.9%.

mx.accuracy: 3.79% and 3.94% average simulation error vs. real hardware (SIMBA and CiM accelerator)
mx.other: Synchronization overhead reduced by up to 99.9% vs. per-cycle sync; 66.1% reduction vs. fixed-quantum sync

th: parallel simulation framework for heterogeneous multi-chiplet systems

t: A. Delegato: Locality-Aware Atomic Memory Operations on Chiplets
pb: Chiplet-based architectures impose high, non-uniform memory access latencies across chiplet boundaries, severely degrading the performance of atomic memory operations (AMOs) used for fine-grained synchronization; existing solutions (near AMOs and centralized AMOs) either cause expensive cache-line ping-pong across chiplets or introduce coherence misses and require ALUs at the directory.
me: The paper introduces two new coherence transactions for far AMOs beyond centralized: (1) Delegated AMOs, which forward the RMW operation via a new SnpAMO snoop to the current cache-line owner, executing the operation locally without cache-line transfer; (2) Migrating AMOs, which transfer cache-line ownership to the requester using an AtomicLoad request (distinguishing it from a ReadUnique for smarter directory tracking). Five static directory AMO policies (All-Central, All-Migrate, Present-Central, Pinned-Owner, Unowned-Central) and a Chiplet-Aware policy are defined based on cache-line state and chiplet location. On top of this, Delegato is a tracing mechanism where the L2 private cache sets a one-bit reuse_bit in every SnpAMO response; the directory's Predictor Table transitions between Pinned-Owner, Present-Central, and Chiplet-Aware states based on this reuse feedback. Evaluated using gem5 23.1 with AMBA 5 CHI protocol, 32 OoO cores (dual 16-core chiplets), and HeteroGarnet NoC.
nv: Delegated and Migrating AMO coherence transactions that enable the directory to execute AMOs at the cache-line owner without invalidation or cache-line transfer, combined with a one-bit reuse tracing mechanism (Delegato) that transports private-cache locality information to the directory predictor.

mx.speedup: 1.07x over centralized AMOs; 1.13x over DynAMO (state-of-the-art AMO predictor)
mx.area: atomic ALU extension: 2894 um2 at TSMC 7nm (0.11% of Neoverse V1 core tile)
mx.other: Delegated AMOs reduce critical-path inter-chiplet messages from 4 to 2 in pathological cases

th: locality-aware atomic memory operation execution on chiplet architectures

t: TileLink: Generating Efficient Compute-Communication Overlapping Kernels using Tile-Centric Primitives
pb: Distributed LLM training and inference require overlapping compute with inter-GPU communication (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter) to hide network latency. Operator decomposition is easy but leaves performance on the table; fusing communication into compute kernels is effective but requires expert CUDA/NVSHMEM code that is error-prone and non-portable.
me: TileLink has a frontend and a backend. The frontend exposes tile-centric primitives: producer_tile_notify/consumer_tile_wait synchronize tile-level data readiness; peer_tile_notify/peer_tile_wait coordinate cross-rank tile dependencies; tile_push_data/tile_pull_data transfer tiles between devices; rank_copy_data/rank_notify/rank_wait handle rank-level collective coordination. The backend performs tile-centric mapping in three stages: (1) shape mapping assigns tile dimensions to compute and communication workloads; (2) rank mapping determines which GPU rank computes/receives each tile via affine transforms (static) or runtime lookup tables (dynamic); (3) channel mapping assigns each tile to an NVLink/InfiniBand channel. The backend compiles these mappings to PTX via Triton extended with NVSHMEM primitives, producing fused kernels that interleave compute threads and communication threads within a single CUDA kernel.
nv: Tile-centric primitive abstraction that decouples compute and communication design spaces at the tile granularity, compiled to overlapping kernels via shape/rank/channel mapping; achieves expert-level overlap with ~10x less code than handwritten CUDA.

mx.vs_flux: Performance comparable to FLUX (expert-written library) with ~200 Python lines vs ~2000 CUDA lines
mx.code_reduction: ~10x less code than equivalent FLUX implementation

th: distributed-compute-communication-overlap

t: Balancing Pipeline Parallelism with Vocabulary Parallelism
pb: In pipeline-parallel LLM training, embedding and output vocabulary layers placed on one pipeline stage cause severe computation and memory imbalance, worsening pipeline bubbles and memory bottlenecks especially for large vocabularies.
me: Vocabulary Parallelism (VP) partitions embedding and output projection layers evenly across all pipeline devices. Computations are grouped into vocabulary-specific pipeline passes. Algorithm 1 reduces cross-device all-reduce barriers from 3 to 2; Algorithm 2 further reduces to 1 barrier by combining online softmax with pre-computed partial gradients. VP integrates with existing 1F1B and V-Half pipeline schedules via a generalizable method.
nv: Online softmax optimization that reduces communication barriers from 3 to 1 within vocabulary layer passes, enabling vocabulary computation to be integrated into existing pipeline schedules with only a small constant activation memory overhead.
th: Pipeline Parallelism / LLM Training Efficiency

t: Radius: Range-based Gradient Sparsity for Large Foundation Model Pre-training
pb: Gradient communication in data-parallel LLM pre-training is a major bottleneck. Existing top-k sparsification methods fail with AdamW (causing divergence) and have poor scalability due to allgather operations whose cost grows linearly with worker count.
me: Radius observes that top-k gradient indices are temporally stable after 15-20% of training steps. It reuses previously computed top-k indices for T steps (T=200 default) to enable dense allreduce on only the top-k fraction of gradients (avoiding allgather). All workers use identical top-k indices (since indices are computed post-allreduce), so only the gradient values need communication without index exchange. Gradient correction (mimicking AdamW operations) is applied before index selection to select indices based on effective model updates. Error feedback accumulates non-top-k gradients for compensation at resampling steps.
nv: Leverages temporal stability of top-k gradient indices to replace expensive allgather with dense allreduce on a sparse subset, making gradient sparsification scalable and compatible with AdamW for the first time.
th: Gradient Compression / Communication Reduction for LLM Training

t: TraceFlow: Efficient Trace Analysis for Large-Scale Parallel Applications via Interaction Pattern-Aware Trace Distribution
pb: Large-scale trace analysis must handle vast datasets; current parallel trace analysis introduces inter-process communications to fetch non-local event data, causing bottlenecks
